title: Infra team wiki: GPU fleet, capacity, cloud accounts, IaC modules, CI/CD and runbooks - Operational Guidance
author: Avery Chen
content:
Overview

This page consolidates operational guidance for the infra engineering team covering: GPU fleet and capacity management, cloud accounts and networking patterns, Terraform/IaC module conventions, CI/CD and build pipelines for infra changes, and runbook excerpts that should live in the team wiki. The guidance is intended to be prescriptive to reduce ambiguity across on-call and project work.

Goals and scope
- Provide a single authoritative reference for day-to-day decisions and escalation paths.
- Cover common scale and failure modes for GPU-backed inference services.
- Document IaC patterns and CI/CD safeguards to maintain fleet stability.
- Surface runbook steps for the most frequent operational actions.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owners: Infra - GPU & Capacity (oncall rotation) and Infra - Cloud Accounts & Networking.
- Pager duty: infra-gpu (primary), infra-networking (secondary).
- Slack channels: #infra-gpu, #infra-networking, #infra-deploys.

High-level architecture assumptions
- GPU fleet is provisioned across 3 cloud regions (us-west-2, us-east-1, eu-west-1) with a mix of T4/A10G/A100 instance types depending on model profile.
- Each region has at least two placement zones for AZ-level resilience.
- Fleet is managed by Terraform modules that provision node pools, instance templates, autoscaling policies, and k8s taints/labels used by serving runtime.
- Networking: VPC per environment (prod/staging/dev) with shared services VPC for cross-environment bastion and monitoring. Transit gateway or cloud-native peering is used for cross-region private connectivity.

Capacity planning (GPU fleet)
1) Key metrics to monitor (SLO-aligned):
   - GPU utilization (p99 / p50 / average) per pool
   - Pod eviction rate (5m, 1h) and OOM events
   - Queue length / request backpressure for the serving runtime
   - Cold-start latency (median, p95) after scale-up
   - Spare instance buffer: configured % of idle GPUs to keep for burst (default 10% for prod)

2) Capacity targets and policies:
   - Production target: sustained 75% average GPU utilization across pools, p95 latency within SLOs.
   - Autoscaling min/max per pool: min determined by baseline steady-state for route partitioning; max set by cost envelope and safety limits.
   - Warm pool and burst capacity: maintain a separate warm pool for models with long GPU initialization (warm_pool_size configurable by model class).

3) Planning cadence:
   - Quarterly capacity review (owners present: GPU capacity lead, runtime, SRE, product).
   - Monthly usage trends report (automated) with forecasts based on 3-month moving average + queued projects.

Cloud accounts and networking guidance
- Account structure: separate cloud accounts for production, staging, dev, and shared infra. Use Organization-level SCPs to limit risky APIs in non-prod.
- VPC design: standardized CIDR allocations per environment using the allocation table below. Avoid overlapping IPs across customer VPCs.

Table: CIDR allocation (example)
| Environment | VPC CIDR | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| prod | 10.10.0.0/16 | GPU node subnets split by AZ: /20 each |
| staging | 10.20.0.0/16 | Smaller pool, mirrors prod layout |
| dev | 10.30.0.0/16 | Unrestricted for dev convenience but restricted outbound egress |

- Networking controls: enforce egress filtering from GPU subnets to avoid uncontrolled data exfiltration; use VPC endpoints for cloud APIs; require flow logs and VPC reachability tests on onboarding.
- Cross-account access: use IAM role assumption with minimal privileges; require approval for any cross-account EC2 or KMS role escalation.

Terraform / IaC module conventions
- Module registry: all reusable modules must exist in the private Terraform registry and follow the naming convention: redwood.<team>.<purpose>. Example: redwood.infra.gpu-node-pool.
- Module requirements:
  - Parametrized inputs only (no hard-coded account IDs or region-specific names).
  - Use version pinning in environment stacks (semver) and prefer patch updates for rolling changes.
  - Each module must include: usage examples, a minimal variables list with descriptions, outputs for critical identifiers, and a migration/upgrade notes section.

- Recommended module list for GPU fleet and networking:
  - redwood.infra.vpc (VPC, subnets, route tables)
  - redwood.infra.gpu-node-pool (instance profile, autoscaler, taints)
  - redwood.infra.instance-template (common tags/iam)
  - redwood.infra.network-peering (transit gateway or peering patterns)
  - redwood.infra.kms (customer master keys and key policies)

- Naming and tagging policy (enforced by pre-commit checks and sentinel policy):
  - resource tags: {team, environment, owner, project, cost-center, infra-stack} as minimum.

CI/CD and build pipelines for infra changes
- Pipeline responsibilities:
  - Linting/formatting: terraform fmt, tfsec (custom rules), checkov for policy level analysis.
  - Unit testing: terratest where applicable for modules.
  - Integration validation: run plan against a short-lived ephemeral workspace (staging account) and run smoke tests (network reachability, instance startup) automatically.
  - Manual approvals: required for production apply (two approvers, one must be from security or SRE when changes touch networking/KMS).

- Gate criteria for terraform apply to prod:
  1) Plan shows only intended changes and no resource replacements without explicit migration notes.
  2) Preflight security scans pass (no high/critical tfsec findings).
  3) Approvals from owners and a designated approver from SRE.

- Build pipeline template (high level):
  1) PR opened against environment stack repo.
  2) CI runs: terraform fmt, terraform validate, tfsec, static checks.
  3) Automated plan in ephemeral workspace; smoke deploy to a disposable staging namespace if stack changes compute.
  4) Request reviewers and get approvals.
  5) Merge triggers a gated run for prod with manual apply and POST-apply smoke tests.

Runbooks and common operational playbooks
- Where to put runbooks: Each runbook must be linked from the team wiki and live under confluence/eng-infra/runbooks with a one-line summary in the team index.
- Runbook template: Symptoms, Impact, Pre-req, Steps (ordered), Rollback/mitigation, Post-incident tasks, Owners.

Example runbook excerpt (GPU node pool scale failure)
Symptoms:
- Autoscaler failed to launch instances; pending pods increasing for > 10 minutes; p95 latency violations.
Impact:
- Affected models experience increased latency or request rejections.
Pre-req:
- Access to cloud console and terraform workspace; SRE on-call availability.
Steps:
1) Confirm pending pods with kubectl get pods -n serving -o wide | grep Pending and check events.
2) Verify cluster autoscaler logs: kubectl logs deployment/cluster-autoscaler -n kube-system --since=15m.
3) Check cloud provider quota and account events (service limits, insufficient capacity errors).
4) If quota or capacity issue, escalate to cloud provider contacts and open a support case; enable temporary burst to alternate region if configured.
5) If autoscaler misconfiguration, roll forward a hotfix in infra modules: run terraform plan/apply in staging, promote to prod with manual approval.
6) If instances are starting but failing health checks, collect instance serial logs and the kubelet logs for the node.
Rollback/Mitigation:
- Move traffic to healthy region with routing policy; scale up warm pool manually using runbook steps.
Post-incident:
- Create incident report: include root cause, timeline, mitigation, and a follow-up action with owner and due date.

Operational checklist for deployments affecting GPU pools or networking
- Pre-deploy: verify module unit tests and plan review, check capacity dashboards for current headroom, notify SRE rotation if change alters autoscaling.
- Day-of: deploy during lower traffic windows by default; announce in #infra-deploys with expected impact window.
- Post-deploy: run smoke tests (model init, throughput sanity), monitor p95 latency for 60 minutes, and confirm autoscaler metrics return to expected ranges.

Audit, telemetry and SLOs
- Telemetry required for capacity decisions:
  - GPU utilization, instance lifecycle events, pod restarts, node conditions, request latency per model.
- Retention: metrics at 1m resolution for 30 days, aggregated rollups (5m/1h) for 365 days.
- SLO examples: serving p95 latency <= 250ms for small models, <= 1200ms for large-batched workloads; error rate < 0.5% per route.

Appendix: quick commands and locations
- Terraform workspace for prod GPU stacks: repo: git@github.com:redwood-infra/gpu-stacks, branch: main.
- Common CI commands: make ci-format, make ci-lint, make ci-plan.
- Dashboards: Grafana -> Infra GPU Overview; Alerts -> PagerDuty infra-gpu.
- Escalation matrix: in runbooks index (link).
